modules.outcome: Write decision, appeal and remedy checks that distinguish closure from whether harm was addressed.

questions.question: A complaint channel requires internet and some workers lack access. Which change addresses the barrier?

options.text: Increase the website font only.
Require everyone to obtain a personal device.
Offer a private offline route with an equivalent response process.
Count offline workers as uninterested.

questions.rationale: Equivalent routes improve practical accessibility.

questions.question: A resident needs to correct an appointment record. What information is appropriate at entry?

options.text: A full personal history for every concern.
Contact details of all household members.
The person’s unrelated medical information.
Information needed to locate and correct the relevant record through the agreed route.

questions.rationale: Collect information in proportion to the issue.

questions.question: A person raises a concern about their supervisor and fears repercussions. What should they learn before submitting details?

options.text: Who sees the report, confidentiality limits and protected alternatives.
Only the number of complaints received last year.
The supervisor’s usual shift pattern.
A guarantee that no information could ever be disclosed.

questions.rationale: People need practical, accurate information to choose a safe route.

questions.question: What is the best evidence that a complainant can track the next step?

options.text: A case folder created with no identifier given.
Receipt with a usable reference, safe contact and a response timeframe.
A notice saying complaints are welcome.
An internal chart that the person cannot see.

questions.rationale: Acknowledgement should make the process navigable.

questions.question: A local mechanism is unavailable for a complaint requiring external authority. What should the practitioner do?

options.text: Require completion of every internal step before offering any information.
Treat the matter as outside all possible remedy.
Explain appropriate external routes and support permitted referral.
Forward it publicly to invite a response.

questions.rationale: Appropriate external routes remain available.

questions.question: A worker fears reprisals for privately raising a concern. How should the report be handled first?

options.text: Require a joint session immediately.
Publish the allegation in meeting minutes.
Treat the concern as a routine scheduling dispute.
Use a protected route and assess safety before considering dialogue.

questions.rationale: A process can intensify risk when power and safety are unresolved.

questions.question: What best shows a participant can freely use a dialogue process?

options.text: They can decline or pause it without a penalty and know other available routes.
They are scheduled by a supervisor.
Their attendance was listed in a public notice.
The facilitator asked them to attend once.

questions.rationale: A real choice requires practical ability to refuse.

questions.question: A vendor asks for the gate to reopen, explaining that early deliveries enable trade. What is the underlying interest?

options.text: A particular gate opening as the sole interpretation.
Reliable delivery access during viable trading hours.
The title of the gate supervisor.
A public vote on all schedules.

questions.rationale: Examining interests can make more options visible.

questions.question: The facilitator can record proposals but cannot change opening hours. What should be clear?

options.text: All suggestions took legal effect as recorded.
The facilitator will approve the change privately.
Who can approve changes and when referral or review will happen.
The parties need no information about the decision-maker.

questions.rationale: A process is credible when authority and timing are known.

questions.question: Two groups try dialogue and retain different views. What should the record show?

options.text: A unanimous agreement because both groups attended.
Only the organiser’s preferred view.
The withdrawal of every prior concern.
Disagreement, open options and relevant next review routes.

questions.rationale: Attendance and discussion do not establish agreement.

questions.question: What makes a grievance decision useful to the person who raised it?

options.text: Reasons, agreed next action, timing and a review route.
A status code with no explanation.
The number of unrelated closed cases.
A reference to all staff email messages.

questions.rationale: The explanation allows the person to understand and challenge the outcome.

questions.question: Eight reports were withdrawn and twelve had remedies implemented. How should these appear?

options.text: Report 20 verified remedies.
Report the dispositions separately and verify remedy outcomes.
Report only referrals and discard both counts.
Combine all cases under evidence of restored access.

questions.rationale: Case dispositions do not establish equivalent results.

questions.question: A manager signs off a replacement path. What further evidence shows it addresses the complaint?

options.text: The work order status turned green.
The path appears in a proposal.
Affected people can use it under the agreed conditions and timing.
More complaints were assigned after it opened.

questions.rationale: Remedy effectiveness concerns whether the change addressed the grievance.

questions.question: A public report’s category could reveal one person’s identity. What is appropriate?

options.text: Publish it alongside the person’s work shift.
Remove the case completely from internal tracking.
Ask all residents to confirm who reported it.
Keep a protected review record and use a safe aggregate in public.

questions.rationale: Separate accountability from avoidable disclosure.

questions.question: Complaint volume rises after a new accessible entry route opens. What should be checked?

options.text: Changes in access, issue frequency and who can report.
Conclude harm necessarily doubled.
Close the new route automatically.
Compare totals without the change date.

questions.rationale: A volume change can reflect access, underlying problems or both.

courses.title: Corporate Accountability and Community Monitoring
courses.school_name: School of Extractive Industries, Livelihoods and SW-EMHEC
courses.audience: Social work learners and practitioners developing extractive-sector community practice skills.
courses.study_guidance: Work from the classroom case records. Refer real environmental testing, clinical assessment, legal decisions and site access to the responsible qualified teams. Complete each practice task before reading the feedback.
courses.practice_safety_note: Work from the classroom case records. Refer real environmental testing, clinical assessment, legal decisions and site access to the responsible qualified teams.
courses.outcome: Trace an extractive-sector commitment to an authorised record, independently assess delivery and propose accountable follow-up.

modules.title: Read disclosed records in context
modules.outcome: Distinguish different kinds of disclosures and check their scope, date and decision relevance.
paragraphs: Transparency can make company and government actions easier to question. A licence record identifies a formal authorisation within a stated scope. A company register may identify a legal entity. A beneficial ownership record concerns who ultimately owns or controls an entity under the applicable reporting rules. A payment record describes a reported transaction. Each record has a different purpose, and a reader needs to know which question the record can answer. Compare relevant fields for identity, dates and scope before drawing a conclusion. [S88]

For extractive work, ask whether a social contribution arises under a legal or contractual commitment or from a discretionary decision. A publicly announced commitment may be recorded by more than one institution, each using different dates or definitions. The EITI requirements distinguish categories of disclosure and how participating countries report them. A missing number should be labelled missing until its meaning is checked. The NEITI solid minerals audit index can guide learners towards official reports, including historical disclosures, once the appropriate reporting period and coverage are checked. [S88] [S91]

Start an evidence log with the source issuing body, record date, period, field and limitation. If one document concerns payment by a company and another concerns receipt by a local body, treat them as different observations until the records can be reconciled. Use the disclosure to formulate a question rather than drawing a conclusion about delivery from only one entry. Request clarification through the appropriate authority. [S88]

The Guiding Principles link reporting to due diligence and remediation. For a practitioner, good reporting helps people see what is changing and access the appropriate remedy. Include information people can act on and protect records that could reveal sensitive case details. [S86]
modules.example: Fictional case: An announcement says a road fund was paid. The audit file shows a commitment, an older disbursement and no record of the current receipt.
modules.activity: Identify what each record establishes. Write a short reconciliation request with the record period, entity and missing confirmation.
modules.feedback: Separate commitment, outgoing disbursement and verified receipt. Check date, scope and entity before reporting a gap or outcome.

modules.title: Monitor delivery and distribution
modules.outcome: Define indicators and verification routes that distinguish resources committed from lived results.
paragraphs: Start with a commitment and describe the benefit as a sequence. A work order, a purchase and an opening date are process milestones. Accessible use by the intended residents is a result that requires its own measure. The monitoring team should state the population, comparison period, unit and practical condition for a successful use. Give the measure a clear owner and explain which evidence can corroborate it. Community contributors can help describe the condition that matters, such as operating before the first shift. [S88]

Build a simple record of planned, approved, delivered and verified stages. Suppose a project approves service for 24 workers and 18 try it. If 12 can use the service routinely, report the fraction of the full approved group and of those who tried it. Record whether each unsuccessful visit reflects capacity, timing, affordability or another barrier. Keep process and result measures separate so a public account can show where delivery is falling short. [S89]

Ask how patterns differ across affected groups and locations. Research on mining-related perceived ecosystem losses in Ghana illustrates why a summary count can miss changed access, household work or cultural practice. An indicator that uses the average across all residents may hide a decline among a group that depended heavily on a service. Seek input from people least able to join the primary monitoring activity and describe limitations proportionately. Preserve privacy by presenting safe aggregates and retaining a protected route for relevant reviewers. [R99]

Agree how discrepancies will be handled. Keep dated accounts with their sources, including cases that contradict a positive picture. Refer physical testing to competent teams and avoid unapproved site access. Define who can make a correction and when to recheck the outcome.
modules.example: Fictional case: An agreement offers 24 workers a service, 18 try it and 12 use it routinely. The contractor reports 100 percent delivery.
modules.activity: Calculate two meaningful rates. Define a corroborating record and an action that addresses an observed timing or affordability barrier.
modules.feedback: Report 50 percent of the approved group and about 67 percent of those who tried it. Verify why planned access did not translate into use.

modules.title: Request correction and verify accountable action
modules.outcome: Prepare a proportionate evidence-based accountability request and specify how correction will be verified.
paragraphs: An accountability request should describe a specific gap and the change the responsible body can make. State the commitment or relevant expectation, the current evidence and who appears affected. Include the area and reporting period and separate observations from open questions. Share a method for providing corrections. Give the responsible body a reasonable opportunity to respond through appropriate channels and preserve access to independent review. Do not present an unexplained discrepancy as conclusive wrongdoing. [S86] [S88]

Use an action register. For each item, set an accountable role, an action, a target date and evidence that would show completion. An answer can acknowledge the concern, contest part of it or commit to a change. Keep these outcomes visible. For a delay in community transport, a proposed new schedule is progress. Verification would require checking that it actually operates and meets the needs of the intended users. Give the community a way to comment on the revised evidence. [S89]

Make a distinction between public reporting and protected case handling. If the request concerns a pattern of access failures, send a minimum supporting summary and share sensitive evidence only under appropriate authority. Review who could be harmed by public disclosure. A reliable grievance channel or independent escalation route can support people who cannot safely attach their names to a public request. Keep records that let an authorised reviewer trace what changed, even if the public summary is aggregated. [S86]

Document whether the correction worked across the intended reach. Identify continuing barriers and reserve a subsequent review. If a result is disputed, acknowledge that the evidence is contested and record how it will be resolved or reviewed.
modules.example: Fictional case: An operator disputes a low service-use figure and offers a new schedule. It asks the team to close the case before checking the schedule.
modules.activity: Write a two-paragraph request with a source boundary, named corrective owner, verification condition and review date.
modules.feedback: Record the disagreement and keep the measure open until the revised route operates and intended users can use it.

questions.question: Which record helps identify who ultimately controls a reporting extractive entity?

options.text: A training attendance sheet.
A notice of community meeting results.
A relevant beneficial ownership record.
A supplier delivery receipt alone.

questions.rationale: Ownership and control information answers a specific transparency question.

questions.question: What should be verified before describing a project payment as mandatory?

options.text: Whether the announcement used a formal banner.
Whether the payment was discussed at a meeting.
Whether the payment amount was rounded.
The applicable legal or contractual basis for the payment.

questions.rationale: The obligation depends on the governing requirement.

questions.question: A 2023 audit amount and a 2025 programme receipt differ. What is the first review step?

options.text: Check period, entity and definition before attempting reconciliation.
Treat the difference as confirmed missing funds.
Copy the larger figure into both records.
Assume the same line is being counted twice.

questions.rationale: Like-for-like comparison is needed to interpret the difference.

questions.question: A field is blank in a disclosure table. How should it be recorded in a learner evidence log?

options.text: Automatically zero for every entity.
Missing or unspecified pending clarification.
Positive because the project announced spending.
Exempt under any possible standard.

questions.rationale: A blank has an unknown meaning until verified.

questions.question: Which public description helps people pursue a delayed benefit?

options.text: Only the programme logo and annual total.
Private payment details for unrelated households.
Scope, expected date, what has been verified and an appropriate follow-up route.
The name of the press release author without details.

questions.rationale: Practical information connects a disclosure with follow-up.

questions.question: Which stage shows a programme is available as advertised?

options.text: The line item was proposed.
The budget was discussed.
A description appeared in a draft.
Confirmed operation at the stated places and times.

questions.rationale: Operations require evidence beyond planning.

questions.question: Twelve of 24 approved workers use a service routinely. What percentage of those approved use it?

options.text: 50 percent.
About 67 percent.
75 percent.
100 percent.

questions.rationale: The approved-group denominator is twenty-four.

questions.question: Some participants arrive after a service closes because of shift hours. How should the monitor record this?

options.text: As universal lack of motivation.
A timing barrier by affected group and relevant attempts.
As successful attendance because attempts were made.
As a budget overrun without evidence.

questions.rationale: Recording the failure mechanism supports a specific correction.

questions.question: The service provider reports successful opening every weekday. Which is a useful independent comparison?

options.text: A logo included in the contract.
The amount written in a press notice.
Dated access reports from an appropriately reached sample of users.
Meeting attendance by procurement staff.

questions.rationale: Independent experience helps test the reported pattern.

questions.question: Publishing exact comments could reveal identities in a small work crew. What should the monitoring team do?

options.text: Publish the full notes with times and names.
Exclude the crew from every analysis.
Change the dates in the source records to conceal them.
Preserve a protected record and publish an appropriately aggregated pattern.

questions.rationale: Safe reporting can retain evidence without exposing identities.

questions.question: Which request is easiest for a provider to verify?

options.text: Compare the signed operating window with dated missed trips for the same route.
Resolve every problem in the region at once.
Confirm that all records are incorrect.
Explain unrelated spending before identifying the programme.

questions.rationale: Bounded requests identify the record and action at issue.

questions.question: Two credible sources conflict about when the service opened. What belongs in the request?

options.text: Only the account that supports the current narrative.
Both dated claims and the evidence needed to resolve them.
An averaged opening date presented as verified.
A finding of wrongdoing based on disagreement.

questions.rationale: Preserve provenance and uncertainty until the conflict is resolved.

questions.question: Who should own a committed timetable correction?

options.text: The person who reported the original failure by default.
Everyone in the community jointly without a role.
The responsible operator or authority able to change it.
The author of a general policy paper.

questions.rationale: Assign an action to a role that can carry it out.

questions.question: A new timetable is printed. What supports closing the access item?

options.text: Type size is larger.
A project memo repeats the proposed hours.
An administrator files the draft schedule.
Evidence the service follows it and the affected users can reach and use it.

questions.rationale: Implementation and use require their own verification.

questions.question: An unresolved pattern includes reports of reprisal. What follow-up is suitable?

options.text: Use a protected referral or independent route with the minimum necessary information.
Attach every named account to a public notice.
Ask complainants to confront the named person in a group.
Delete all evidence to close the dashboard item.

questions.rationale: A safe route keeps sensitive evidence available for the right reviewer.

courses.title: Extractives Community Intervention Practicum
courses.school_name: School of Extractive Industries, Livelihoods and SW-EMHEC
courses.audience: Social work learners and practitioners developing extractive-sector community practice skills.
courses.study_guidance: Work from the classroom case records. Refer real environmental testing, clinical assessment, legal decisions and site access to the responsible qualified teams. Complete each practice task before reading the feedback.
courses.practice_safety_note: Work from the classroom case records. Refer real environmental testing, clinical assessment, legal decisions and site access to the responsible qualified teams.
courses.outcome: Produce and defend a phased, reviewable intervention for fictional Afirin Ridge using assessment, referral, engagement and accountability evidence.

modules.title: Assemble a case evidence brief
modules.outcome: Combine different evidence streams and identify priority questions, affected people and decision owners.
paragraphs: The final practicum brings several observations together without collapsing them into a single story. Work from the fictional Afirin Ridge file. Early case notes report route delays near a project, a future closure threatens paid and informal work, and a separate service complaint remains unresolved. Treat each issue according to its evidence and urgency. Begin with a table of affected groups, changes reported, records available and questions that could change a decision. [S85]

Add a boundary statement describing place, time and population for each question. Road access may affect residents and mobile vendors at different times. Project employment records may exclude informal suppliers. A caregiver’s report can identify a clinic access barrier while a qualified agency investigates possible environmental harm. Document which claims are reported, independently supported or unresolved. Compare facts that refer to the same period and activity, then connect related issues through plausible mechanisms. [S89]

Draw a simple theory of change for one proposed response. If a revised route and suitable timetable enable people to reach a market or service, verify safe access and operating times before measuring changes in attendance or earnings. Identify assumptions, including affordability and uptake. Evidence from the 2026 Ghana and Australia policy comparison encourages a check of social support and work transition alongside physical closure work. Make the assumptions local to the fictional brief. [R96]

Finish with a priority and ownership map. Give early attention to a time-sensitive support need and to evidence that could uncover severe or hard-to-reverse loss. Clarify the practitioner’s part and the roles responsible for clinical, environmental and land decisions. Preserve review options for people who challenge an entry.
modules.example: Fictional case: Afirin Ridge has a route complaint, a threatened loss of informal trading and a health concern supported only by testimony.
modules.activity: Create a brief with four affected groups, two observed or reported patterns, three evidence gaps and the authorities or teams responsible.
modules.feedback: Give each question a purpose and owner, separate support and causation, and include people whose work is missing from registers.

modules.title: Compare and rehearse intervention options
modules.outcome: Compare two responses using practical access, protection, feasibility and authority, then test exception cases.
paragraphs: Choose two feasible responses and describe what would happen under the current arrangement. A route adjustment with temporary support can be compared with a new transport service and a separate transition plan. Use the same criteria for each, including practical access, residual loss, operating costs, safeguarding and timing. State which benefits are provisional. Identify the body that would authorise each relevant change and who can influence the decision. [S85] [S87]

Run a tabletop exercise with fictional scenarios. Include a typical case, a person who needs a protected contact, a supplier who missed the eligibility list and a user who cannot attend at the proposed time. Give each scenario an expected result and a person responsible for recording what occurred. Check whether the referral is received, the alternative route actually works and the affected person can ask for independent review. Use the same case definitions when comparing an amended plan. [S86]

Consider a new claim during the exercise. A provider may produce a statement that says a route is operating while people describe being unable to use it. Treat the claim as new evidence with a scope and date. Examine alternative explanations and verification options, then determine whether a qualified review is needed. Do not discard adverse results just because a sponsor prefers the proposed arrangement. Be clear about who can decide and how the response will be communicated. [S88]

Write a conditional recommendation. Name one change that can proceed within the team’s scope and a condition that would pause a wider decision. Include an accessible fallback and a date for retesting observed failures.
modules.example: Fictional case: A tabletop trial works for most participants. A vendor missing from the list is refused help, and a confidential callback is redirected to the wrong desk.
modules.activity: Compare two options, label the two failures, assign corrective owners and specify what would justify pausing expansion.
modules.feedback: Correct eligibility review and protected contact. Keep the failures in the evidence record and use the same scenarios in the retest.

modules.title: Defend the decision and review plan
modules.outcome: Present a phased decision memo integrating all eight EIL domains with accountable review.
paragraphs: A decision memo should explain what can proceed, what requires conditions and who must decide. Start with a dated account of the fictional project stage and affected groups. Show why the recommended option handles the most important needs. Include one viable alternative and explain the evidence that could reverse the choice. Give the social work team and qualified authorities distinct roles. Use language appropriate for both a supervisor and a community briefing. [S85]

Include conditions that address livelihood and displacement concerns. Describe which work and resources people may lose, how an alternative would be accessed and which benefit promises require separate verification. State the role of transition timing and support. Add a protected referral route and a separate grievance process, including a way to review a disputed response. Note how the affected people could challenge both the evidence and the implementation plan. [S86] [S87]

Provide a decision table with indicator, group, timing, source, owner and trigger. Connect each line to the underlying decision. A financial commitment can support a question about capacity, while actual access requires evidence about use. For transparency review, distinguish commitments, payments and delivery and cite the proper public records where relevant. Protect case identities while recording evidence privately for authorised review. [S88]

Prepare to defend one finding that supports the memo and one that limits it. Explain how failure cases would be handled and which results might update the plan. Define follow-up dates and communication routes so a reviewer understands when the next decision will be made and what records would substantiate it.
modules.example: Fictional case: The sponsor asks for immediate rollout after 8 of 10 routine scenarios succeed. Both attempted cases with the least access fail.
modules.activity: Write a one-page decision with an alternative, permission boundaries, two review measures and a specific condition for retesting.
modules.feedback: Use bounded revision or pause. Keep both denominators, verify the protected fallback and state who owns the next review and when.

questions.question: How should the practicum brief record a resident’s first description of a route delay?

options.text: Verified average delay for all users.
A confirmed cause from site testing.
Reported experience, with time and place and an appropriate check.
An observed delivery of a remedy.

questions.rationale: An account supports enquiry without resolving other evidence questions.

questions.question: A proposal concerns a service trip at two locations and only on market days. How should the brief bound the sample?

options.text: By the entire population without a time period.
By office staff only.
By a publication year without a route definition.
By the affected market trips, locations and relevant timing.

questions.rationale: The scope must match the decision and pathway.

questions.question: Which group needs its own case entry when the employment list excludes regular vendors?

options.text: The vendors who depend on project-related foot traffic.
Only permanent supervisors.
The owners of unrelated properties.
A duplicate group of direct employees.

questions.rationale: The work dependency extends beyond a payroll list.

questions.question: Which assumption should the brief test when a new shuttle is expected to restore market attendance?

options.text: The shuttle provider has a name.
The service runs at the right times at a price affected users can pay.
Every resident travels for exactly the same purpose.
A printed route always proves attendance.

questions.rationale: The service needs practical access for the theory of change to hold.

questions.question: The brief contains a technical contamination question and an agreed service request. How should work be organised?

options.text: Delay agreed support until all technical evidence is final.
Use the same practitioner decision as proof of both.
Refer technical assessment to the qualified body and progress consented support separately.
Share personal records publicly to resolve uncertainty.

questions.rationale: Separating tasks allows safe action while technical review proceeds.

questions.question: What makes two intervention options comparable in the practicum?

options.text: Use net costs for one and turnout for the other.
Remove the current arrangement from the decision context.
Apply access criteria only to the preferred option.
Assess both against the same affected groups, time period and criteria.

questions.rationale: Common criteria and conditions support a fair comparison.

questions.question: Which fictional test complements one successful mainstream shuttle journey?

options.text: A worker who cannot pay the proposed fare and needs the early service.
The same journey repeated with unchanged conditions only.
A pricing discussion with no intended user.
A vote asking whether transport matters.

questions.rationale: Exceptions reveal who might fail outside the ordinary path.

questions.question: The drill reveals that a private callback is routed to an unsuitable desk. What is the immediate finding?

options.text: Completed access because a dial tone was heard.
A confidentiality process failure needing correction and retest.
Proof every referral system is unsafe.
A publishing success because the case reached someone.

questions.rationale: The exercise checks whether safeguards work in practice.

questions.question: A sponsor shares a claim of reliable service without a record period. How should the practicum handle it?

options.text: Treat it as verified for all users.
Overwrite all user reports.
Record the claim and ask for dates, scope and corroboration.
Assume the claim is false before review.

questions.rationale: Qualification keeps the evidence open without overstating it.

questions.question: Which condition warrants pausing expanded use of the fictional pathway?

options.text: A corrected logo is awaiting approval.
The team used different pens at the meeting.
One editor wants another page heading.
A protected-contact failure remains unresolved after rehearsal.

questions.rationale: An unresolved safeguard failure can change whether expansion is responsible.

questions.question: Which memo opening supports clear action after the tabletop reveals unresolved problems?

options.text: Describe the bounded revision, decision owner and condition for reconsideration.
List all scenario titles without a recommendation.
Request a launch relying only on majority results.
Mark every decision as already authorised.

questions.rationale: A good memo states the action and its conditions.

questions.question: Eight of ten routine cases succeed and zero of two low-access cases succeed. What evidence should the memo show?

options.text: Ten successes without individual groups.
Both group results with their denominators.
A single claim that every scenario worked.
The routine count with the low-access results erased.

questions.rationale: Disaggregated outcomes reveal a material access failure.

questions.question: Which monitoring line can an authorised reviewer act on?

options.text: An objective with no time or owner.
A cost estimate with no action linked to it.
Group, period, evidence source, named owner and adjustment trigger.
Only a headline on the number of meetings.

questions.rationale: A traceable line connects evidence and a decision.

questions.question: Who should decide whether a technical restriction can be lifted in the fictional memo?

options.text: The exercise facilitator based on presentation quality.
The provider based only on commercial need.
The first stakeholder to attend the review.
The authorised qualified decision-maker using their applicable review criteria.

questions.rationale: Technical decisions need the appropriate authority and evidence.

questions.question: What should a learner include when defending a conditional recommendation?

options.text: The finding or failed assumption that would change the choice.
A commitment never to change the proposed route.
A claim that no future evidence is relevant.
Only the benefits observed in routine cases.

questions.rationale: Reviewable decisions make thresholds and uncertainties explicit.
